transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I'm here because I just can't seem to get my sleep back on track, and it's starting to really interfere with my work. You see, I've always been an incredibly disciplined sleeper. As a chief executive, I have to be. I usually have a strict routine—in bed by 10:30, asleep by 11:00, up at 6:00 sharp, ready to tackle the day. I've operated like that for years, decades even. But lately, well, ever since my cousin passed away recently... it's all just fallen apart. 

I try to go to bed at my usual time, but I just lie there in the dark. My mind won't shut off. I keep replaying that entire night over and over again in my head, every little detail, every sound, every horrible moment. It just loops. And when I finally do manage to drift off, it's not restful. I'll jolt awake at 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, my heart racing, because I'm having these... these flashes, these awful scraps of images from the hospital. The lights, the machines, the look on the nurses' faces. It's just so vivid. Once I'm awake like that, there's no going back to sleep. I just lie there until my alarm goes off. 

And the result is that I'm going into these high-stakes board meetings, where I need to be sharp and decisive, feeling completely fragmented. It's like I've only slept in pieces, you know? I'm exhausted, I'm foggy, and I just can't afford to be operating at half capacity right now. I thought it would just pass, that I'd get over the shock and go back to normal, but it's just not happening, and I really need to get my sleep schedule sorted out before it starts affecting the company.
Have you been avoiding places, people, or activities that remind you of your cousin's passing?

No, not really. I mean, I haven't been avoiding anything specifically. I still go to the office every day, I still take my usual route to work, I still have my regular lunch meetings at the club. I haven't canceled any of my obligations. In fact, I've been trying to lean into my routine, to keep things as normal as possible, because that's how I operate. I believe in structure. I believe in facing things head-on. 

So, no, I haven't been staying away from people or places. I haven't avoided talking to my family, although, to be perfectly honest, I haven't really had the time to sit around and dwell on it with them either. I've just been pushing through, trying to get back to business as usual. It's just... it's just this sleep issue, this constant replaying of things in my head when I'm trying to rest, that's the real problem. The rest of my life, my schedule, my interactions, they're all exactly as they were. I just need to fix the sleep so I can actually be present for all of it.
Do you feel like this sleep issue and the thoughts about your cousin's passing are significantly impacting your daily life or relationships?

Well, yes and no. I mean, as I said, I'm still going into the office, still keeping up appearances. I haven't dropped the ball on the major, high-stakes board meetings—the ones where my presence is absolutely non-negotiable. I'm still showing up for those, still putting on the suit and sitting at the head of the table. But... if I'm being completely honest, and I suppose I have to be if we're going to fix this, it *is* taking a toll. It's just bleeding into things in ways I really despise. 

Because of this exhaustion, this absolute lack of quality rest, I've actually had to start delegating some of my other responsibilities. I'm on the board of a couple of local charities, community obligations that I usually take a lot of pride in handling personally, but I've had to pass those off to my VP. I just don't have the bandwidth. And my workdays... I've had to shorten them. I used to be the first one in and the last one out, a solid twelve-hour day, minimum. Now, by 3:00 or 4:00 PM, I'm just hitting a wall. I have to pack up and go home because I'm just not as steady, you know? I'm not as sharp or effective when I'm dealing with people in the late afternoon. I get irritable, I lose my train of thought, and as a CEO, you simply cannot let your team see you falter like that. You have to project absolute confidence and stability. So, yes, while I'm still functioning on a macro level, the micro level is definitely suffering. The edges are fraying, and it's incredibly frustrating because I am used to operating at 110%, not 70 or 80.
Do you feel guilty about your cousin's passing?

Guilty? No. No, I don't feel guilty. I mean, why would I? It wasn't my fault, it was a medical issue. A terrible, sudden medical issue. I certainly didn't cause it, and I couldn't have prevented it. I'm a chief executive, doctor, not a cardiologist. I manage companies, I don't manage arterial blockages or whatever it was that finally gave out on him. 

I suppose... I mean, people always talk about survivor's guilt or wishing they had done more, but I'm a very pragmatic person. I deal in facts and actionable items. The fact is, he was in the hospital, he was receiving the best care available—I made sure of that, I personally called the hospital administrator to ensure he had the top specialists—and despite all of that, his body just failed. There was no action I could have taken to change the outcome. 

So, no, there's no guilt. There's just... well, there's just this intense frustration with the aftermath. The shock of it, the visuals of that night in the ICU, the way it's disrupted my entire equilibrium. It's the loss of control that bothers me, not guilt. I'm used to being able to fix things, to strategize and execute a plan to resolve a problem. But you can't strategize your way out of death, and you apparently can't strategize your way into a good night's sleep when your brain decides to go rogue. That's the issue here. Not guilt, just a profound, exhausting lack of control over my own mind at 3:00 AM.
Are there any specific memories or thoughts about your cousin's passing that you try to push away or not think about?

Push them away? No, no, I don't do that. I really don't. You see, that goes entirely against my nature. As I was saying earlier about how I operate, I am someone who confronts issues directly. If you have a problem in a company—say, a critical failure in a merger or a sudden drop in quarterly earnings—you don't just close your eyes, plug your ears, and pretend it isn't happening. You look at the raw data, no matter how ugly it is. 

So, when the memories of that night come up... the hospital room, the harsh fluorescent lighting, the sound of the machines... I don't try to shove them into some dark corner of my mind. I don't actively try to block them out or distract myself. I just let the thought happen. I acknowledge it as a factual event that occurred. I mean, what good would it do to try and suppress reality? It happened. He's gone. I'm a mature woman, I know that avoiding the truth is a completely ineffective strategy. 

If a memory crosses my mind while I'm sitting at my desk, I just think, "Yes, that was a tragic situation," and I attempt to return to my work. I don't run from it. The issue—and this is what I keep coming back to—is just that at night, my brain decides to review these files, so to speak, on a continuous loop when I need to be resting. But as for consciously trying to push the thoughts away or refusing to think about them? No, absolutely not. I believe in facing the music, always have. People who try to bury things... well, I've found they usually end up making a much bigger mess of things later on. You simply have to look facts in the eye, whether you like them or not.
Do you feel anxious most of the time, even when there's no apparent reason to be?

Anxious? Well, I wouldn't use the word anxious, exactly. Anxiety implies a sort of... irrational fear of the unknown, doesn't it? A sort of nervous fluttering about things that might never happen. I am not a nervous flutterer. But... there is a certain heightened state of alertness that I've noticed, a kind of constant, low-level vigilance that I just can't seem to shake off. It's not anxiety, it's more like my system is stuck in an 'on' position, scanning for threats that aren't there.

It's most pronounced when I'm driving, actually. I commute every day, same route I've taken for the last ten years, but lately... lately it feels entirely different. When I drive now, I keep checking the mirrors, constantly. I find myself hyper-aware of the speed of the trucks around me, calculating their trajectory, wondering if they're drifting out of their lanes. I even catch myself actively looking for where I could pull off the road if there was a sudden emergency, scanning the shoulders and the exits. And this is on familiar roads to the office, roads I could navigate in my sleep! Yet, my body stays incredibly tight, my grip on the steering wheel is white-knuckled, and my shoulders are practically up by my ears. It's as if I’m just waiting for something terrible to happen, bracing for an impact or a disaster that, logically, I know isn't coming. It's exhausting, frankly. I get to the office and I feel like I've already put in a full day's work just getting there safely. So, while I wouldn't call it 'anxious' in the traditional sense, there is definitely this persistent, physical tension and hyper-awareness that has completely taken over my routine.
Do you often find yourself worrying about everyday things, like work or finances, even when there's no obvious reason to worry?

Worrying about everyday things? Work or finances? Oh, absolutely not. No, no, no. I mean, my goodness, if I started worrying about the day-to-day operations of the firm or whether the quarterly projections are going to align with the board's expectations, I wouldn't have survived in this industry for thirty years. I am the chief executive. My entire job is to handle those things, to manage the risk, to foresee the financial pitfalls and steer the ship around them. I don't sit around wringing my hands over the budget or the supply chain. I execute. I delegate. I problem-solve. 

Honestly, I find that sort of petty worrying to be a complete waste of cognitive energy. If there's a financial issue, you look at the ledger, you find the discrepancy, and you rectify it. You don't sit on your sofa at home fretting about it. And my personal finances? Please. I have a very capable wealth manager who handles my portfolio, and frankly, I'm at a stage in my career where I don't need to look at price tags. So, no, the mundane, everyday things... the bills, the office politics, the standard operational hiccups... they don't cause me a moment's hesitation. 

That's what makes this whole situation so incredibly infuriating, doctor. I am perfectly capable of handling a multi-million dollar merger without breaking a sweat. I can stand in front of a hostile board of directors and command the room. But now, I'm gripping the steering wheel like a terrified teenager just driving down Interstate 95 because my brain is suddenly convinced a semi-truck is going to merge into my lane. It's the lack of logic in it that I despise. I don't worry about the things I *should* be managing, the things that actually require my attention and expertise. I'm just dealing with this... this bizarre, physical overreaction to absolutely nothing. So, to answer your question, no. Everyday worries are not on my radar. I am far too pragmatic for that.
Do you ever feel like you're reliving the night your cousin passed away, as if you're right back in the hospital room?

Reliving it? Like I'm actually back there? No, I wouldn't say I lose touch with reality or hallucinate that I'm standing in the ICU. I am very grounded in the present moment. I know I am sitting here in your office, just as I know when I am sitting in my boardroom or my living room. I don't have flashbacks like you see in the movies where the veteran hits the deck because a car backfires. 

But... and this is the frustrating part, because it interrupts my workflow... there are these incredibly sharp, sudden intrusions. They aren't memories I'm choosing to access. It's more like... well, it happens at the most odd moments. For instance, if my phone rings late at night. Even if it's just an automated alert from the overseas markets, which happens all the time given our interests in Tokyo and London. The moment that specific ringtone chimes in the dark, it's not just a thought that crosses my mind; it's a completely vivid, high-definition picture of that hospital corridor that just shoves its way into my brain. The specific shade of that awful, sterile green paint on the walls, the smell of the antiseptic, the exact tone of the police officer's voice when he first approached me... it just pushes in. 

Or, as I was mentioning about my commute, if I'm driving home late from a dinner meeting and the glare of headlights from oncoming traffic hits my rearview mirror in a certain way... boom. The image of the wrecked car, or the flashing lights of the ambulance, it just flashes right over whatever I'm currently looking at. It's so abrupt and so vivid that I actually have to pause what I'm doing. If I'm walking, I have to stop. If I'm driving, I have to take a deep breath and physically steady myself, grip the wheel tighter, and consciously remind myself, "You are driving on Route 4, you are fine." It's a momentary derailment. I have to actively re-route my brain back to the present task. It's highly inefficient, frankly. I don't like things that hijack my attention without my permission. So, while I'm not "reliving" it in a delusional sense, these sharp pictures definitely force their way in and demand a pause, whether I have the time for it or not.
Are there any specific activities or situations that you've been avoiding because they remind you of your cousin's passing or the events surrounding it?

Avoiding? No. No, I don't have the luxury of avoidance, doctor. My schedule is dictated by the needs of a very large, very demanding organization, and it is set months in advance. I can't simply decide to stop doing things or changing my routine because they make me uncomfortable. That’s just not how I operate. 

Take the driving, for instance. I told you how awful the commute has become, how I'm gripping the wheel and hyper-fixating on the trucks and the headlights. A perfectly reasonable person might decide to take the train for a while, or hire a driver, or take some winding backroad to avoid the highway. But I don't. I get in my car every single morning at 6:15 AM, and I drive that exact same stretch of Route 4, and I merge onto Interstate 95, just like I have for a decade. Taking a detour would add at least twenty-five minutes to my commute, and twenty-five minutes is an eternity in my morning. I have a 7:30 AM briefing with my executive team every day, without fail. I am not going to be late to my own meeting because I was trying to avoid a stretch of pavement. 

And the phone calls... I mentioned how the late-night ringtone triggers that... that vivid picture of the hospital. I could just turn the phone off, couldn't I? Put it on silent, leave it in the kitchen. But I don't. I can't. The overseas markets don't care that I had a traumatic experience with a midnight phone call. If the Nikkei drops, or if there's a supply chain disruption in our London office, I am the one who needs to make the call on how we respond. So, the phone stays right on my nightstand, volume up, exactly where it's always been. 

Even the hospital itself... actually, just last week, the wife of one of my senior Vice Presidents had a rather complicated bypass surgery. Guess which hospital she was at? The exact same one. The very same facility they took my cousin to. Now, did I want to go there? Absolutely not. Just the thought of walking back into that building made my chest tight. But it is expected of me, as the head of the firm, to show support. It's about leadership, about optics and morale. So, I had my assistant buy an absurdly expensive floral arrangement, I got in my car, and I drove there. I walked right through those same automatic sliding doors, walked right past that dreadful sterile green paint on the walls, and I did what was required of me. I smiled, I shook hands, I made small talk with the VP in the cafeteria. 

So, no, I am not avoiding anything. I am doing exactly what I have always done. It requires a ridiculous amount of cognitive override right now, and frankly, it is exhausting to have to force myself through these motions while my body is apparently convinced we are in imminent danger. But I push through it. I execute the day just like I always do. Avoidance is for people who have the option to step back, and I simply do not.
Are there any specific people you've been avoiding because they remind you of your cousin's passing?

Avoid people? No. Look, as I was just explaining about the hospital visit, avoidance simply isn't in my vocabulary, and that applies to people just as much as it does to places or situations. I mean, who would I even avoid? My family? My staff? It’s completely impractical. 

After he passed, his immediate family was... well, they were an absolute wreck. Understandably so, of course, but they were entirely paralyzed by the grief. Someone had to step in and manage the logistics, and as usual, that fell to me. I was the one on the phone with the funeral director, the estate attorneys, the people at the hospital... I handled it all. If I started avoiding anyone who reminded me of that night, I would have had to cut off my entire extended family. And frankly, they were relying on me to steer the ship. They needed someone who could keep a clear head, and I am not going to abandon my family just because looking at them makes me uncomfortable.

And then there’s the office. Obviously, my executive team knows what happened. My assistant handled the influx of condolence cards and the changes to my calendar that week. I can’t exactly avoid my own assistant or my VP, can I? I have to walk in there, look these people in the eye, accept their sympathies with grace, and then immediately pivot the agenda back to our quarterly targets. Do I enjoy seeing the pity in their eyes, knowing they associate me right now with a personal tragedy? No, I despise it. It's a distraction. 

And yes, does seeing his mother—my aunt—bring back a flash of that awful hospital waiting room? Yes, absolutely. I get that same tight feeling in my chest that I mentioned earlier, that completely illogical physical spike. But I don't turn around and walk the other way. I walk right up to her, I take her hand, and I do what is required of me as her niece. So, no, doctor. I am not avoiding anyone. I am interacting with exactly who I need to interact with, precisely when I need to interact with them. I refuse to let this... this ridiculous glitch in my nervous system dictate my schedule or my relationships. I just push through it, same as everything else.
Do you often find yourself being overly alert or on edge, even in situations where most people would feel safe?

Alert? Well, I suppose you could call it that, though I would probably describe it as being inefficiently, exhaustingly hyper-focused. But yes, absolutely. I mean, I brought up my commute a moment ago, that drive down Route 4 and I-95. Now, I have driven that exact stretch of pavement thousands of times. I know every merge lane, every curve, every single traffic pattern. It should be—and for the last ten years, it has been—a completely mindless drive. A safe drive. It's usually my time to mentally organize the agenda for my 7:30 AM briefing and review my talking points. 

But now? Now it is an entirely different, incredibly frustrating experience. When I get behind the wheel, it’s like my brain just... it completely overrides my logic. When I drive now, I keep checking the mirrors, constantly. I mean, darting my eyes back and forth every few seconds. I find myself obsessively monitoring the speed of the trucks around me—and there are always so many massive commercial trucks on 95 at that hour—calculating their distance, their speed, and actively scanning the shoulder to figure out exactly where I could pull off if one of them suddenly swerved or blew a tire. 

It’s completely irrational. I am driving on highly familiar roads, making my standard morning run to the office, a route I could practically do in my sleep. There is no logical reason for me to feel threatened. And yet, the entire time, my body stays incredibly tight. My shoulders are practically up to my ears, my grip on the steering wheel is so tight my hands actually ache by the time I arrive at the parking garage, and my jaw is just clamped shut. It’s exactly as if I’m just... waiting for something to happen. Waiting for an impact that isn't coming. It takes a massive amount of conscious effort to remind myself that I am perfectly safe in my own vehicle, and quite frankly, having to spend my morning commute managing my own nervous system instead of preparing for my workday is a terrible use of my time.
Do you feel an overwhelming fear or anxiety when you encounter reminders of your cousin's death?

Overwhelming? No. No, I wouldn't use the word overwhelming, doctor. Overwhelming implies that I am somehow incapacitated by it, that it stops me from executing my duties or functioning normally, and as I think I've made abundantly clear by now, absolutely nothing stops me from doing what needs to be done. 

Fear isn't really the right word for it, either. I mean, look at that hospital visit I just told you about, with my Vice President's wife. When I walked through those automatic sliding doors and smelled that terrible clinical antiseptic smell, I didn't feel terrified. I wasn't having some sort of dramatic panic attack or looking for a place to hide. What I felt was... well, it was that tight, restrictive sensation in my chest that I mentioned earlier. Just a sudden, completely illogical spike in my heart rate, and a very intense, very clear desire to just turn around, get back in my town car, and return to my office where things actually make sense and are under my control. 

But anxiety? Overwhelming fear? No. It’s just this deeply, deeply frustrating physical reaction that I have to actively manage. It’s like my body is trying to send me a high-priority warning signal about a threat that simply does not exist, and I have to use my conscious mind to just... override it. To tell my nervous system to stand down. 

The same goes for the phone ringing late at night. I don't wake up paralyzed by terror. I wake up, my pulse is elevated, and I have a split-second flash—a very visceral, very annoying memory of that specific night with my cousin. But then my logic immediately kicks in. I look at the screen, I see the country code for the London office, and I answer the call. If I were overwhelmed by fear every time I encountered a trigger, I wouldn't be able to run a firm of this size. I'd be curled up in bed, and that is simply not an option for someone in my position. 

So, to answer your question, no. I don't feel overwhelming fear. What I feel is a heightened, highly irritating state of physical tension that requires entirely too much mental bandwidth to suppress. It's an internal management issue, really. I just need to figure out how to optimize my physiological response so I can stop wasting so much valuable energy on it. But I am certainly not overwhelmed.
Have you noticed any significant problems in your relationships with others due to your current symptoms?

Significant problems? Well, I suppose it depends entirely on how you define a relationship problem, doctor. I am certainly not getting into shouting matches with my family or breaking down crying in front of my board of directors, if that is what you mean. I maintain my professionalism at all times. 

However... I will concede that my usual dynamic with people has shifted, and it is incredibly bothersome to me. I am still showing up for the most essential meetings, of course. The quarterly financial reviews, the high-level strategy sessions with my executive team, the final sign-offs on major acquisitions—those are absolutely non-negotiable. I am physically in the room, sitting at the head of the table, steering the conversation exactly as I always do. 

But my interactions during those meetings... they lack their usual precision. I have to admit that I’m just not as steady or effective with people as I normally am. Usually, I can read a room instantly. I know exactly how to push my Vice President of Sales to get better margins, I know how to reassure anxious shareholders, and I can navigate the subtle nuances of a complex negotiation without breaking a sweat. Lately, though, I find my patience with people is practically non-existent. I'm uncharacteristically brusque. I find myself rushing through conversations and cutting people off just to get them out of my office so I can close the door and stop having to process their input. It's not fair to my staff, and quite frankly, it's terrible leadership on my part. I pride myself on being a very steady hand at the wheel, and right now, I feel like I'm white-knuckling my way through every single interpersonal interaction.

Because of this unsteadiness, I've had to make some highly uncharacteristic adjustments to my calendar. I've actually been shortening my workdays, which I absolutely despise doing. Leaving the building at 5:00 PM instead of my usual 7:30 PM feels like a complete dereliction of duty, but I simply do not have the mental stamina to maintain my composure with my colleagues for those extra hours right now. By the late afternoon, the effort it takes to look people in the eye and pretend I'm not entirely on edge is just too much. 

And on top of that, I’ve had to completely delegate my community obligations. Usually, I am the face of the firm at the local Chamber of Commerce dinners, the hospital charity galas, the university endowment boards. I excel at that kind of networking; it's a vital part of maintaining the firm's relationships in the city. But right now? The mere thought of standing in a crowded ballroom making small talk with fifty different people, having to maintain that perfectly polished, steady facade while my nervous system is humming like a high-tension wire... I just can't do it. I've had my Communications Director step in to cover all my public-facing events this month. It’s a strategic retreat, I suppose, to protect the firm's image while I deal with this, but it is immensely frustrating to have to manage my professional relationships this way.
Do you ever feel like you're detached from yourself or the world around you?

Detached? No. No, doctor, quite the opposite, actually. If anything, I am entirely too anchored to every single thing happening around me. Detachment implies a sort of... floating away, doesn't it? A disconnect from reality or a sense of unreality. I assure you, I am firmly, stubbornly planted in reality. My problem isn't that I'm drifting off; my problem is that reality is currently demanding an utterly unreasonable amount of my cognitive resources just to process standard, daily inputs. 

When I sit in my office, I am acutely, almost painfully aware of everything. I notice the exact pitch of the HVAC system kicking on, I hear the specific, strained tone my executive assistant uses when she’s fielding a difficult call from the press, I feel the exact texture of the leather on my desk chair. I don't feel disconnected from my body at all. As I mentioned earlier with the muscle tension and the jaw clenching, I am highly aware of my physical state because I am constantly having to manage it. 

I mean, I suppose I can understand the mechanics of it—why someone going through a difficult time might just... check out mentally. A sort of psychological resignation to protect themselves from the stress, letting their mind wander off to some safe, quiet place. But I have never operated that way, not in business and not in my personal life. As a chief executive, you simply do not have the luxury of checking out. You have to be present, you have to be engaged, and you have to be the one steering the ship, regardless of the weather. 

So no, I don't feel detached from myself or the world. I feel like I am aggressively micromanaging my own physical and mental existence right now, and quite frankly, it is exhausting. I am entirely too present, if you want my honest assessment.
Do you have memories of your cousin's passing that feel like they are happening all over again, as if you are reliving them?

Reliving them? Like some sort of cinematic flashback where I completely lose touch with my surroundings? No, doctor, I think I've already made it clear that I am firmly planted in reality. I am not hallucinating that I am back in that night. 

But I will admit that I am experiencing these... interruptions. Highly vivid, deeply annoying interruptions. They happen at the most odd, completely inconvenient moments, usually when my mind isn't fully occupied with a complex work task. I mentioned the phone ringing late at night earlier, which is certainly a primary offender. But it can be something even more mundane than that. If I'm being driven home from the office, for instance, and I happen to look out the window and see the sudden glare of headlights from the oncoming traffic on the highway—just that specific intensity of light hitting the glass—it's as if my brain simply bypasses all my executive functioning.

In that split second, a perfectly sharp, entirely uninvited picture of that hospital corridor just pushes its way into my mind. The exact color of the walls, the terrible lighting, all of it. Or, sometimes I'll suddenly hear the police officer’s voice. Not just a vague recollection of what he said, but the actual, precise cadence and tone of his voice, echoing right there in my head as if he were sitting next to me in the car. 

It is incredibly jarring. It completely derails whatever I was thinking about, and I literally have to stop, close my eyes, and pause to steady myself. I have to take a very deliberate breath and actively force that image, that sound, back into its proper place so I can regain my equilibrium. It’s the sheer inefficiency of it that bothers me the most, frankly. I am used to my mind being a highly organized system. I pull up the information I need, exactly when I need it. I do not appreciate these memories just kicking the door down without my authorization. It takes a considerable amount of effort to recalibrate my focus after one of those moments, and quite frankly, I do not have the time or the patience to be pausing to steady my nerves every time a set of headlights catches my eye.
Are there any memories or thoughts related to your cousin's passing that you try to avoid thinking about?

Avoid them? No. No, avoidance really isn't in my repertoire, doctor. I... well, I suppose I understand why some people might try to just bury their heads in the sand when something awful happens, but I have built my entire career on confronting issues directly. If there is a crisis at the firm—a bad quarter, a sudden shift in the market, a supply chain failure—I don't pretend it isn't happening. I gather the data, I look it right in the eye, and I deal with it. 

So, no, I am not actively trying to avoid thinking about my cousin or the circumstances of his passing. I mean, honestly, what practical good would that do? It happened. It is a factual, undeniable reality that I have to integrate into my life now, whether I like it or not. Now, do I enjoy thinking about the hospital corridor or the police? Obviously not. It is highly unpleasant and, as I just mentioned, incredibly disruptive to my schedule. But I don't try to shove those thoughts into a box and lock them away. 

I think... well, if you sit there and try to avoid thinking about a pink elephant, all you are going to do is think about a pink elephant, isn't that how the psychological principle goes? It just seems like a massive waste of mental energy to try and block things out. When the thoughts come, I acknowledge them. I just try to process them efficiently so I can get back to my work. I face things. That is simply how I operate, both professionally and personally. So, as far as intentionally dodging thoughts or memories of him... no, I haven't been doing that at all.
Are there any memories or thoughts about your cousin's passing that you find yourself trying not to think about?

Doctor, I believe you just asked me that exact question a moment ago, didn't you? Yes, I'm quite certain you did. As I was just explaining—and I do apologize if I wasn't clear enough the first time, I know I can sometimes get caught up in the details of my own methodology—but as I was saying, no. I do not try to avoid thinking about it. 

I understand that repetition is a standard part of these assessments, ensuring you get a consistent baseline, but my answer remains exactly the same. I don't avoid the memories. I don't avoid the thoughts. It is simply contrary to my entire way of functioning in the world. As I detailed just a minute ago, if there is a problem, if there is an unpleasant reality, my approach is to look at it directly. I don't hide from it. I don't try to distract myself with television or hobbies or whatever it is people do when they want to pretend something hasn't happened. 

I am a fifty-eight-year-old woman who runs a major corporation. You do not get to this position by running away from uncomfortable facts. So, whether it's the thought of the phone ringing, or the police, or my cousin himself, I do not actively try to push those thoughts away or avoid them. They are there, they are facts, and I deal with them as they arise, however inconvenient they may be to my schedule. So, to answer your question again, no, I am not trying to avoid thinking about it.
Do you feel like your reaction to your cousin's passing is disproportionate to what might be expected from someone in your situation?

Disproportionate? I... well, I suppose that depends entirely on what you consider "expected," doesn't it? I mean, what is the standard metric for grief?
